body:
# Independent audit: projective three-cap overlap in every dimension

Auditor: `minkowski_transfer`. Verdict: **PASS** for
`candidate 2338b9b22d6faa2f`, including its
nonsymmetric inverse-power radial lemma, density tightening, and all
normal-rank branches. I also independently read the entire dependency
`candidate d2f8ecd6d2f1309c`.

This proves an ordinary continuous-volume overlap inequality. It does
not preserve a sampled mixed-integer source under the projective map.
No such assertion is used in this audit.

## 1. Radial bounds, attainment of ray integrals, and continuity

The lower bound for phi on its open convex domain is justified by the
small-ball contradiction: mixing a point of value epsilon with a fixed
ball on which phi<=A produces a ball of radius proportional to epsilon
with phi<=2epsilon. Its integral lower bound is proportional to
`epsilon^(r-beta)`, which diverges because beta>=r+1>r. No disjointness
of these balls is needed, since each single integral is bounded above
by the fixed finite total mass.

The convex sublevel at twice phi(0) contains a ball and has finite
volume. An unbounded convex set containing a ball contains cones of
arbitrarily large volume, so this sublevel is bounded. Choosing R to
enclose it and interpolating from zero to a point beyond R gives the
claimed linear lower growth of phi. Together with the positive lower
bound on phi in the remaining bounded region, this yields the global
polynomial upper tail on f. It is sufficient at the exact endpoint
beta=r+1, without a strict inequality beyond that endpoint.

The fixed interior ball gives a positive uniform lower bound for I
on the unit sphere, and the tail gives a finite uniform upper bound.
Along a ray from an interior point of an open convex domain there is
at most one boundary parameter. All larger parameters are outside the
closure; otherwise contraction toward the interior origin would give
an interior point beyond the purported endpoint. Consequently the
pointwise convergence needed for dominated convergence fails at most
at this one parameter. The tail dominates the ray integrands uniformly,
proving continuity on the sphere and then continuity of the gauge at
zero by homogeneity and the uniform bounds.

## 2. The nonsymmetric quantile proof

For I(x)=I(y)=1, the positive densities on the two ray intervals are
continuous and strictly positive. Their increasing quantile functions
are C1 at every v in (0,1), with the stated derivatives. Each quantile
tends to zero as v decreases to zero. The harmonic interpolation T
is strictly increasing, and the identities

    a+b=1,   aR+bS=T,   aRx+bSy=Tz

hold exactly. Direct differentiation gives

    T' = T [a/(R^r f(Rx)) + b/(S^r f(Sy))].

Multiplication by `T^(r-1) f(Tz)` and convexity of phi yield exactly
its displayed lower bound. Weighted Holder with exponents beta and
beta/(beta-1) gives the first estimate, and the concavity exponent
`r/(beta-1)<=1` gives the second. No symmetry, mode, or centroid
condition enters. At equality beta=r+1 the latter step is simply
linear and remains valid.

Integrating over v in (0,1) covers the increasing interval traced by
T, which is contained in the positive ray of z. The integral is at
most I(z), so the pointwise lower bound one proves I(z)>=1. If z=0,
convexity of the gauge at that point is immediate from its definition.
For other points, homogeneity extends the unit-boundary chord assertion
to the entire unit sublevel. The radial bounds make this sublevel a
compact convex body containing zero in its interior.

The factor r in the final radial-body definition is correct: polar
integration of body volume uses `rho^r/r`. It gives precisely the
original total mass and the mass in every through-center halfspace,
including the correct orientations. No section-speed reweighting is
needed for this mass-preserving transfer.

## 3. Concurrent tightening for unbounded density support

The compact-body dependency has a valid cap-tail inverse, correct
positive-circuit image hyperplane, and exact common-upper-level
functional monotonicity. This monotonicity is not a coordinatewise
monotonicity claim: above the original minimum only the sum decreases;
below that minimum the functional is `(m-r)t`. Therefore its stated
strictness for r<m is correct.

For the inverse-cubic density, all proper cap tails are continuous by
absolute continuity, strictly decreasing on the interior projection
interval, and have unique continuous finite inverses at proper mass
levels. A fixed interior point has a positive cap tail in every
nonzero direction. Thus sufficiently small positive mass levels put
all three thresholds beyond that point's scalar products. Their
positive weighted sum is then positive, supplying a finite crossing
without a bounded-support assumption. The tightened caps remain
subsets of the original caps and cover the whole plane.

If their concurrence lies outside or on the boundary of the convex
support, separation puts the support in a closed halfplane through
that point. The two-cap assertion used here is valid, including its
closed boundary: on the angular semicircle, each concurrent halfplane
restricts to an initial interval, a terminal interval, the whole
interval, or at most the two endpoints. In the last case the other
caps cover the interior and hence, by closedness, its endpoints as
well. Otherwise retain the longest initial and terminal intervals;
because the original intervals cover, these two cover the entire
semicircle. Hence the remaining cap's mass is a lower bound for the
overlap. Interior concurrence is handled directly by the radial body.

## 4. BBL hypothesis and exact projective Jacobian

I independently checked the ordinary primary background statement,
Bobkov, *Convex bodies and norms associated to convex measures*,
Lemma 2.3, in the source linked by the proof:
https://www-users.cse.umn.edu/~bobko001/papers/2010_PTRF_Norms.pdf.
Its functional BBL form has no symmetry premise and gives the exponent
`p/(1+kp)` when k variables are integrated. The positive-endpoint
convention permits zero densities outside a convex support.

The affine coordinates have two v coordinates, one t coordinate,
and D-3 y coordinates. In `(z,t,y)` with v=tz the Jacobian is t^2.
After t=1/s and y=w/s the three factors are respectively s^-2,
s^-2, and s^(-(D-3)), giving exactly s^(-(D+1)). There are D-2
integrated variables `(s,w)`. Thus

    p=-1/(D+1)>-1/(D-2),
    p/(1+(D-2)p)=-1/3.

The perspective domain is convex: mixing transformed points with
weights alpha,1-alpha corresponds to mixing their original points
with weights alpha*s_1/s and (1-alpha)*s_2/s. These are positive and
sum to one. The inverse power of the density is s on this domain.
All BBL hypotheses therefore apply.

Bounded original K gives a uniform upper bound on F from the formula
integrating `t^2` over fixed bounded t and y ranges. The projective
image of int(K) is open, full-dimensional, and convex. For precise
application of the radial lemma one may restrict the density to this
open positive interior and set it to zero on the support boundary.
That boundary has planar Lebesgue measure zero, so all total and cap
masses are unchanged. The BBL inequality and inverse-power convexity
hold on this open domain. This clarification avoids presuming that
section-density representatives are positive only on an open set.

The t=0 part is a hyperplane section of a full-dimensional body and
has ordinary D-volume zero. Fubini and the genuine changes of real
variables preserve every original cap mass. The fixed affine-coordinate
Jacobian multiplies every mass by one positive scalar and does not
alter inverse-cubic convexity. Unbounded projective support is permitted.

## 5. Separation, all normal ranks, and sharpness

A two-cap subcover immediately gives overlap at least the remaining
cap mass. Rank one also gives a two-cap subcover by keeping the strongest
half-line of each orientation. In rank two, the ordinary projected
volume density is log-concave, hence inverse-cubic convex. Planar Helly
applied to the support and three strict complements gives either a
two-cap subcover of the support or a whole-plane cover. In the latter
case absence of a two-cap subcover forces a minimal positive circuit.

For rank three, the margin image is full-dimensional and compact.
Separation from the open negative orthant gives a nonnegative nonzero
coefficient vector and a nonnegative weighted margin throughout K.
If a coefficient vanished, the other at most two caps would cover K.
Thus all coefficients are positive. Rank three permits the declared
affine coordinates, with all three margins homogeneous in (v,t) and
weighted sum t. Their projective forms have weighted sum one, so they
cover the whole plane. Their projected normals have rank two: otherwise
the original three forms in (v,t) would have rank at most two. The
positive dependence is minimal for the same reason; no zero projected
normal or hidden one-cap trace is overlooked.

The preceding density theorem proves the desired coefficient 3/4 in
all ranks. Closed boundary masses require no extra correction in this
ordinary setting: all nonzero boundary normals cut Lebesgue-null
hyperplanes, and all transformations were applied to the density
itself. The triangle product equality example preserves each cap
fraction and total volume, proving sharpness in every D>=2.

No substantive error was found. The audit requests only the explicit
open-support representative and angular-semicycle clarifications above;
they justify steps already valid in the source rather than alter its
conclusion. No projective statement about integer fibers is inferred.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
